L2478@P105: authorized under specifications dated August
L2479@P105: 25, 1975 which remained in use until replaced
L2480@P105: by the Battle Dress Uniform (BDU) in the mid1980s.
L2481@P105: In 1963, tropical combat clothing was type
L2482@P105: classified for production and issue to soldiers
L2483@P105: serving in Vietnam. There were three basic
L2484@P105: patterns of Tropical Combat Coats. The first
L2485@P105: was made of olive green shade 107, wind
L2486@P105: resistant cotton poplin with two slanted
L2487@P105: bellows-type breast pockets and two bellows
L2488@P105: type lower pockets on the coat. The pockets
L2489@P105: had flaps secured by two exposed plastic
L2490@P105: buttons, an interior button over gas flap,
L2491@P105: shoulder loops, and a double button adjustment
L2492@P105: tab on each side at the waist. The second pattern coat was the basically the same as the first
L2493@P105: pattern except that all of the buttons were covered to prevent snagging in jungle terrain.
L2494@P105-106: 103Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2495@P106: A second pattern Coat, Combat,
L2496@P106: Tropical, Wind Resistant in OG-197
L2497@P106: cotton poplin.
L2498@P106: A third pattern Coat, Combat,

L2502@P106: Resistant (Class 2), in cotton ripstop.
L2503@P106: By 1967 a third pattern coat (Class 1) was standardized in either olive green shade 107, wind
L2504@P106: resistant cotton poplin or olive green shade 107, cotton rip-stop. This coat retained the slanted
L2505@P106: pockets with hidden buttons, but the shoulder loops, gas flap, and adjustment tabs were
L2506@P106: eliminated. A second pattern of this coat (Class 2) in Engineer Research and Development
L2507@P106: Laboratory (ERDL) camouflage was produced in cotton rip-stop. This uniform was issued to
L2508@P106: pathfinders, long range reconnaissance patrol members and scout/reconnaissance personnel.
L2509@P106: Each of these uniforms had matching trousers with slanted front pockets, rear pockets with flaps,
L2510@P106: and bellows-type cargo pockets with flaps on the legs.
L2511@P106: Effective July 14, 1966, the Department of the Army directed that both tapes have black lettering
L2512@P106: on an olive green shade 107 background. In 1967 rank insignia worn on the Tropical Combat
L2513@P106: Coat began being changed over to a subdued pattern of black on olive green. In 1968, all
L2514@P106: insignia, Army wide, worn on the field jacket, utility uniform and the tropical combat uniform
L2515@P106: was changed to the subdued black on olive green. In addition, the Personnel Armor System for
L2516@P106: Ground Troops (PASGT), consisting of a Kevlar helmet and a ballistic vest, was also introduced
L2517@P106: in the early 1980s. The PASGT Helmet replaced the M1 and M1C Steel Helmets for both
L2518@P106: ground troops and parachutists. The system first saw use in combat in 1983 during Operation
L2519@P106: Urgent Fury in Grenada, but most soldiers did not receive the Kevlar until a year or two later.
L2520@P106: In 1967 rank insignia worn on the Tropical Combat Coat began being changed over
L2521@P106: to a subdued pattern (black on olive green). In 1968, all insignia, Army wide, worn
L2522@P106: on the field jacket, utility uniform and the tropical combat uniform was changed to
L2523@P106: subdued. Rank insignia for enlisted personnel was moved from the sleeve to the
L2524@P106: point of the collar.
L2525@P106-107: 104Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2526@P107: 
L2527@P107: Above is a selection of insignia showing the change over from bright to subdued which began in 1967.
L2528@P107: On October 1, 1981 the Army introduced the Battle Dress Uniform or BDUs as they are called.
L2529@P107: This uniform was descended from the tropical combat uniform of the Vietnam War and consisted
L2530@P107: of a coat made of a nylon and cotton blend in woodland pattern camouflage with matching
L2531@P107: trousers, and a field cap. Because combat experience in Grenada showed that the BDU uniform
L2532@P107: was too hot for tropical climates, the Army authorized the wearing of the old tropical combat
L2533@P107: uniform for several years while adjustments were made.
L2534@P107: By 1988, a hot weather version of the BDUs in cotton rip-stop was available. The two uniforms
L2535@P107: were very similar in style, with a coat that had four straight bellows-type pockets each with a flap
L2536@P107: secured by hidden plastic buttons, and matching trousers with slanted front pockets, rear pockets
L2537@P107: with flaps, and bellows-type cargo pockets with flaps on the legs. With only minor stylistic
L2538@P107: changes such as the elimination of the waist adjustment tabs, the reduction of the size of the
L2539@P107: collar, and refinements in stitching and fit, BDUs were worn until replaced by the Army Combat
L2540@P107: Uniform in 2006.
L2541@P107: Members of the 3rd Infantry in 1987. The soldier on
L2542@P107: the left is wearing the OG-107 tropical combat
L2543@P107: uniform authorized for wear until the woodland
L2544@P107: camouflage Battle Dress Uniform as worn by the
L2545@P107: soldier on the right could be fielded.
L2546@P107: The Army also introduced a Desert Camouflage
L2547@P107: Uniform (DCU) at the same time as the woodland
L2548@P107: pattern BDU, but issue was limited to special
L2549@P107: operations troops, and soldiers assigned to
L2550@P107: exercises in the Middle East such as Operation
L2551@P107: Bright Star in Egypt. The uniform was virtually
L2552@P107: the same as the BDUs but in a six-color tan, brown
L2553@P107: and black desert camouflage pattern. Six-color
L2554@P107: DCUs have come to typify the American soldier in
L2555@P107: the Persian Gulf War (1991), although due to
L2556@P107: logistics glitch issue of the desert uniform to
L2557@P107: soldiers (especially those in VII Corps), was very
L2558@P107: restricted. The Army began issuing a new threecolor Desert Camouflage Uniform in July 1991.
L2559@P107: This uniform was worn by troop participating in
L2560@P107: Operation Enduring Freedom, and Operation Iraqi
L2561@P107: Freedom from 2002 to 2006, when it was also
L2562@P107: replaced by the Army Combat Uniform.
L2563@P107-108: 105Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements

L2582@P108: The Army Combat Uniform (ACU) was officially established as the combat and garrison
L2583@P108: uniform for the Army on 14 June 2004, and has replaced both the Battle-Dress Uniform and the
L2584@P108: Desert Camouflage Uniform. The ACU consists of a coat, trousers, black beret or matching
L2585@P108: patrol cap, moisture wicking T-shirt, moisture wicking socks, and brown combat boots.
L2586@P108-109: 106Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2587@P109: The color scheme is composed of a gray, tan and sage green digital pattern. The color black was
L2588@P109: omitted from the uniform because it is not commonly found in nature and appears excessively
L2589@P109: dark when viewed through night vision goggles.
L2590@P109: The ACU Coat is single breasted with integrated blouse
L2591@P109: bellows for increased upper body mobility, and a plastic
L2592@P109: zipper closure that can be opened from either the top or the
L2593@P109: bottom with a front placket that covers the zipper and is
L2594@P109: secured by hook and loop (Velcro) fasteners. The coat has a
L2595@P109: Mandarin collar that can be worn up or down; tilted breast
L2596@P109: pockets with hook and loop closure; a three-slot pen pocket on
L2597@P109: the bottom of the left sleeve; and hook and loop sleeve cuff
L2598@P109: closures. On each sleeve near the shoulder there is a slanted
L2599@P109: pocket with a hook and loop covered flap closure, each with
L2600@P109: an integrated infrared identification square on the outside.
L2601@P109: Below each sleeve pocket there an elbow pouch for an
L2602@P109: internal elbow pad insert.
L2603@P109: Rank insignia is attached to a hook and loop patch located on
L2604@P109: the front center of the coat. Both the name tape and the US
L2605@P109: Army tape are attached above the left and right pockets
L2606@P109: respectively and are removable. In the future it will be much
L2607@P109: more difficult to positively identify Army uniforms since unit
L2608@P109: patches and the national identification insignia (US flag) are
L2609@P109: attached by hook and loop rather than being sewn in place.
L2610@P109: The Digital camouflage Army
L2611@P109: Combat Uniform with matching
L2612@P109: patrol cap with the insignia of a
L2613@P109: Private First Class of the 3rd Infantry
L2614@P109: Division.
L2615@P109: Only metal pin-on qualification badges are authorized for wear with this uniform. The matching
L2616@P109: trousers have forward-tilted cargo pockets; Knee pouches for internal knee pad inserts;
L2617@P109: drawstring leg cuff; and bellowed calf storage pocket on the left and right leg.

L2643@P110: with a relatively new product known as the hook and loop fastener or by its commercial name of
L2644@P110: “Velcro.”

L2646@P110: pattern

L2648@P110: camouflage pattern
L2649@P110: Beginning in 1982, with the introduction of the Battle Dress Uniform, the Army began
L2650@P110: manufacture of the M65 field coat in woodland pattern camouflage and desert camouflage
L2651@P110: pattern material. Subsequently, manufacture of the field coat has incorporated the changes of
L2652@P110: camouflage patterns as the have occurred, three color desert pattern in 1991 and universal pattern
L2653@P110: digital in 2005. The latest version has hook and loop patches for the attaching of the name tape,
L2654@P110: US Army tape, shoulder sleeve insignia, and rank.
L2655@P110: The M-1951 field cap was made of wind resistant poplin and was a slightly modified version of
L2656@P110: the original cap adopted in 1943. The M-1951 had a slightly longer visor with rows of
L2657@P110: reinforced stitching. For cold weather use, the cap had a flannel-lined fold-down flap that
L2658@P110: covered the ears and the back of the head. A number of senior officers considered the M-1951
L2659@P110: field cap to be too slovenly for a proper soldierly appearance. Unit commanders often required
L2660@P110: the cap to be worn with cardboard or various commercially available stiffeners inside, to keep it
L2661@P110: straight and upright. In 1953 this policy became official throughout the Army when Chief of
L2662@P110: Staff General Matthew B. Ridgeway began directing forces to improve their soldierly image.
L2663@P110: Commercially manufactured stiffened and blocked models of the field cap were produced and
L2664@P110: sold through the Post Exchange that met military appearance standards. The preferred model
L2665@P110: was the "Spring-Up" manufactured by Louisville Cap Corporation. These caps became
L2666@P110: universally known as “Ridgeway Caps.” While the M-1951 field cap remained standard issue,
L2667@P110: use of the Ridgeway cap became widespread throughout the 1950s.
L2668@P110-111: 108Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2669@P111: The M1951 Field Cap The “Spring-Up" model of the “Ridgeway Cap”
L2670@P111: manufactured by Louisville Cap Corporation
L2671@P111: In 1958 the Army established a headgear study group to find a replacement for the unsatisfactory
L2672@P111: M-1951 field cap. The peacetime conditions during the 1950s had led to an emphasis on
L2673@P111: appearance. In January 1962 a new cap design was adopted known as the “Cap, Field, Hot
L2674@P111: Weather.” The term “hot weather” was used because the cap did not have earflaps. The new cap
L2675@P111: was a “baseball” style, made of olive green shade 106, polyester and rayon blend, with a soft
L2676@P111: visor and a rounded crown constructed of six triangular segments meeting at the top. There was
L2677@P111: a ventilation eyelet in each segment. It its original form, the cap was almost universally disliked.
L2678@P111: The polyester and rayon material proved to be too hot in tropical climates, and soldiers did not
L2679@P111: like the look of the high curving front panel. Soldiers either crushed the front of the crown to
L2680@P111: improve its appearance or purchased theater-made replacements with a lower front panel and a
L2681@P111: small button at the top of the crown. Eventually a newer version of the cap without the button
L2682@P111: was introduced for issue at the very end of the Vietnam era. The hot weather field cap continued
L2683@P111: in use until it was finally replaced in 1985. The M-1951 style field cap, referred to as a “patrol
L2684@P111: cap” was reintroduced as part of the Battle Dress Uniform in woodland and desert camouflage
L2685@P111: material, and was continued as part of the Army Combat Uniform in universal digital
L2686@P111: camouflage pattern.

L2697@P112: Vietnam as a substitute for the field cap, but
L2698@P112: their use was frowned upon by higher level
L2699@P112: commanders, since they were also considered
L2700@P112: “unmilitary” looking. Similar hats, known as
L2701@P112: “Hat, Combat, Desert Camouflage Pattern,
L2702@P112: were introduced as part of the Desert
L2703@P112: Camouflage Uniform, and were used
L2704@P112: extensively during the Persian Gulf War
L2705@P112: (1990-1991).

L2708@P112: On June 14, 2001, the black beret was authorized for
L2709@P112: wear with the utility uniforms (the BDU, maternity
L2710@P112: BDU, aviation BDU, desert BDU, hospital duty
L2711@P112: uniform, food service uniform, flight uniform, combat
L2712@P112: vehicle crewman uniform and cold weather uniform)
L2713@P112: and the service uniforms (class A and B uniforms).
L2714@P112: With the introduction of the Army Combat Uniform
L2715@P112: the wearing of the beret was extended for wear by
L2716@P112: trainees and while assigned to a combat zone.
L2717@P112: Left: An official Army photo showing the proper wearing of the

L2719@P112-113: 110Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2720@P113: Production of the M1 Steel Helmet was resumed in 1951. The helmet retained all of the features
L2721@P113: of the helmets made at the end of World War II except the color was changed to olive drab shade
L2722@P113: 319 which more closely resembled the olive drab shade 7 used for field equipment. The new
L2723@P113: helmets were equipped with an olive drab shade 7, T-1 chin strap, with metal clips to allow
L2724@P113: removal and a ball and claw buckle quick release buckle. In 1966, the color of the helmet was
L2725@P113: changed to Munsell (Munsell color order system) Y10, a lighter shade of olive green, and in
L2726@P113: 1973 the T-1 chinstrap was replaced with a cotton and nylon web chinstrap with a chin cup,
L2727@P113: adjustment buckles on both sides, and black triangular clips that attached to the bail on each side
L2728@P113: of the helmet.
L2729@P113: A post-1950 production M1 Helmet in

L2736@P113: In 1955 a new resin impregnated cotton liner was introduced
L2737@P113: with a heaver olive drab shade 7, web suspension inside, and
L2738@P113: with the insignia eyelet eliminated from the front. The
L2739@P113: helmet liner was modified in 1963 with the eliminated of the
L2740@P113: leather chinstrap and the addition of a new neck band held in
L2741@P113: place by three metal buckles. At the same time, an identical
L2742@P113: liner made of nylon was introduced and both were produced
L2743@P113: simultaneously until 1969, when a nylon liner with a
L2744@P113: removable inside web suspension held by clips attached to
L2745@P113: metal dish-shaped studs, became standard. This liner was in
L2746@P113: use when the M1 helmet became obsolete in 1988.
L2747@P113: 
L2748@P113: The U.S. Marine Corps developed a new reversible camouflage helmet cover in 1959, made of
L2749@P113: heavy cotton twill with a green, brown and black leaf pattern on one side and a mottled tan and
L2750@P113: brown pattern on the other. The cover had two rows of buttonholes for inserting foliage to break
L2751@P113: up the lines of the helmet. Used with the cover was the olive drab elastic camouflage helmet
L2752@P113-114: 111Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2753@P114: band that was introduced during World War II. In accordance with a DoD directive, the cover
L2754@P114: was issued to the Army beginning in 1961. The cover was modified slightly in 1966, being
L2755@P114: printed on a lighter weight cotton duct with a slightly deeper gap between the two middle flaps to
L2756@P114: add clearance for the chip strap of the helmet. Starting in 1971 a non-reversible helmet cover in
L2757@P114: ERDL (Engineer Research and Development Laboratory, Natick, MA), woodland pattern
L2758@P114: camouflage began replacing the reversible covers. The new cover was darker with more brown
L2759@P114: than previously. After 1980, the helmet band was manufactured and issued with two luminous
L2760@P114: plastic reflectors stitched to one side at the seam. Finally, in 1983 this cover was modified
L2761@P114: slightly, being printed in a somewhat lighter shade of color and on a heaver cotton and nylon
L2762@P114: blend cloth. Both patterns continued in use until the M1 helmet became obsolete in 1988.

L2773@P114: In 1982, the Army introduced the Personnel Armor System for Ground Troops (PASGT), which
L2774@P114: consisted of a Kevlar helmet and a ballistic vest. Kevlar is the DuPont Company's registered
L2775@P114: trade-name for a light, strong spun synthetic fiber. The system first saw use in combat in 1983
L2776@P114: during Operation Urgent Fury in Grenada, but most soldiers did not receive the system until a
L2777@P114: year or two later.
L2778@P114: The PASGT Helmet was shaped similar to those worn by the German Army in World War II and
L2779@P114: was designed to replaced the M1 and M1C Steel Helmets for both ground troops and
L2780@P114: parachutists. The helmet came in five sizes from extra small to extra large and provided ballistic
L2781@P114: protection for the head from fragmenting munitions and handgun bullets. It came with an
L2782@P114: integrated strap suspension system inside the helmet and two-point chin strap that could be
L2783@P114: upgraded to a four point chinstrap and pad suspension system for airborne use. The color of the
L2784@P114: helmet was a light olive green and it was accompanied by a helmet camouflage cover and band
L2785@P114: in either woodland pattern camouflage or desert pattern camouflage (six-color or later threecolor) as appropriate.
L2786@P114: The ballistic vest was made of spun Kevlar and was produced with a woodland pattern
L2787@P114: camouflage outer shell. A desert (six-color or later three-color) camouflage pattern cover could
L2788@P114: be added as needed. Throughout 2003 and 2004 the army began replacing the PASGT helmet
L2789@P114: and body armor with the Advanced Combat Helmet and the Interceptor body armor system.
L2790@P114-115: 112Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements

L2798@P115: The Advanced Combat Helmet (ACH) is based on the Modular Integrated Communications
L2799@P115: Helmet (MICH) design and provided increased 9mm bullet protection. The helmet came with a
L2800@P115: pad suspension system and a four-point chinstrap. The design has less flare than the PASGT
L2801@P115: helmet to allow for increased head mobility. The MICH was a special operations ballistic helmet
L2802@P115: that incorporated protection with the ability to interface with most tactical headsets and
L2803@P115: microphones used by the Special Operations Command.
L2804@P115: The Interceptor body armor is ballistically superior to the PASGT with bullet stopping
L2805@P115: capabilities. The system consists of an outer tactical vest (OTV) lined with Kevlar and two small
L2806@P115: arms protective inserts (SPPI). The vest was tested to stop a 9 mm round with minimal
L2807@P115: deformation. In addition the Interceptor body armor has add-ons such as a groin apron for
L2808@P115: increased protection. The vest was originally issued with a woodland camouflage pattern outer
L2809@P115: shell, but this was later replaced with desert and universal pattern shells. It also had a PALS
L2810@P115: webbing grid on the front of the vest which could accommodate the Modular Lightweight Loadcarrying Equipment (MOLLE) or items of All-purpose Lightweight Individual Carrying
L2811@P115: Equipment (ALICE) equipment.

L2822@P115-116: 113Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2823@P116: Some design problems with the Interceptor led the Army to adopt the Improved Outer Tactical
L2824@P116: Vest (IOTV) in 2007. In addition to increased protection, the IOTV was designed to take the
L2825@P116: weight off the shoulders and move it to the lower torso of the wearer. It was also equipped with
L2826@P116: a mesh inner cover designed to improve airflow. There was a cushioning pad in the lower back
L2827@P116: area of the vest designed to mitigate back injuries due to impact or blunt force trauma. Also, the
L2828@P116: entire armor system was able to be released with the pull of a hidden lanyard, providing a quick
L2829@P116: means for escape in case the wearer became trapped or fell into water. Like the Interceptor the
